metadata.note: Santa Fe's route into Lubbock from the north: Amarillo – Canyon – Happy – Tulia – Kress – Plainview – Hale Center – Abernathy – Lubbock, about 120 miles. Built by the Pecos and Northern Texas Railway, a Santa Fe subsidiary from 1901: Canyon–Plainview opened February 27 1907 and Plainview–Lubbock on January 9 1910, which is when Lubbock got its Santa Fe connection. The Panhandle and Santa Fe Railway leased the P&NT on June 5 1914 and absorbed it in 1948; the P&SF was itself merged into the AT&SF on August 1 1965. The passenger service was trains 93 and 96 -- the West Texas Express westbound, the Eastern Express eastbound -- worked in the early 1950s by articulated motor car M-190, then from 1955 (train 96 renumbered 94) by conventional trains with coaches and sleepers connecting at Amarillo with the San Francisco Chief. Discontinued June 19 1965. NOT DRAWN HERE: Lubbock was also a stop on Santa Fe's Coleman Cutoff (Sweetwater–Coleman opened December 1 1911, Farwell–Lubbock Junction March 1 1914), over which trains 65/66/75/76 -- the California Special -- ran Galveston/Houston – Temple – Brownwood – Sweetwater – Lubbock – Slaton – Clovis – California from February 7 1915 to July 18 1968. That route is a separate corridor and is not part of this layer, so Santa Fe passenger service at Lubbock actually outlasted the line drawn here by three years.
geometry_sources: OpenStreetMap via Overpass API (maps.mail.ru mirror), bbox 33.48,-102.15,35.32,-101.50, all railway=* ways. Corridor-weighted Dijkstra over a 25 m node-merged graph between Amarillo and Lubbock, corridor defined by the nine geocoded station towns. 999-point raw path, spike-cleaned and Douglas-Peucker simplified at 25 m to 106 points, 123.4 miles.
Nominatim geocoding for the nine station towns.
metadata.not_yet_sourced: No timetable was consulted, so every headway_min and the avg_speed_kmh are estimates; the 1440-minute figures are inferred from trains 93/96 being a single daily round trip. Service frequency before 1948 is entirely unknown -- the 720-minute figures for 1910-1948 are guesses. The date passenger service on this specific branch began is assumed to be the January 9 1910 line opening; no source was found confirming scheduled passenger trains from that date. Whether the alignment was ever relocated between 1910 and 1965 has not been checked against a period valuation map.

properties.line: Panhandle and Santa Fe: Amarillo – Lubbock
properties.speed_source: Estimated. No Amarillo–Lubbock schedule time was found for any era; 55 km/h is a plain guess for a 123-mile line with eight intermediate stops.
properties.geometry_quality: Fully real-traced from OpenStreetMap -- no straight-line approximation anywhere on this feature, and no bridged gaps over 60 m. 146.3 km of the trace is BNSF Railway's Plainview Subdivision (the ex-Santa Fe Canyon–Plainview–Lubbock line), 16.8 km is BNSF's Hereford Subdivision over the Amarillo–Canyon stretch the two routes share, 20.7 km is untagged rail (yard and connecting track at Amarillo and Lubbock), and about 1.6 km is other named track at the Amarillo terminal throat. Traced length 123.4 miles against a documented 120 miles (Amarillo–Canyon about 17, Canyon–Plainview 57 opened February 27 1907, Plainview–Lubbock 46 opened January 9 1910); the 3 percent excess is normal curvature against round milepost figures. The trace passes within 1.1 km of all eight documented station towns (Amarillo 0.07, Canyon 0.42, Happy 0.19, Tulia 0.94, Kress 0.10, Plainview 1.07, Hale Center 0.44, Abernathy 0.40, Lubbock 0.32 km). Five yard-detour spikes were removed and the result carries no reversal over 120 degrees and no revisits. CAVEAT: this is today's BNSF alignment. The corridor is believed unrelocated since construction, but no period valuation map was consulted, and the exact terminal trackage into the Amarillo and Lubbock depots in 1910-1965 is not the same as the yard layout drawn here. Straight-line repair 2026-08-29: 2 ruled segments totalling 26 mi replaced with OpenStreetMap-traced rail geometry (see geometry_repairs for the OSM lines each one followed).

segments.note: The Pecos and Northern Texas Railway, a Santa Fe property since the AT&SF bought it in 1901, reached Lubbock on January 9 1910 with the 46-mile line up from Plainview, completing a through route from Amarillo south through Canyon (Canyon–Plainview, 57 miles, had opened February 27 1907). Lubbock's rail connection to the Santa Fe system dates from this line. headway_min and avg_speed_kmh are estimates, not read off a timetable.
sources: Segment-level: the January 9 1910 Plainview–Lubbock opening (46 miles), the February 27 1907 Canyon–Plainview opening (57 miles) and the AT&SF's 1901 acquisition of the P&NT are given in the Texas State Historical Association's P&NT entry; headway and speed are unsourced estimates.

segments.note: The Panhandle and Santa Fe Railway took the name on June 5 1914 and leased the P&NT's properties, so this line was worked by the P&SF from then on. In the same year the P&NT completed the 88-mile Farwell–Lubbock Junction line (March 1 1914), which with the Sweetwater–Coleman line of December 1 1911 made Lubbock a crossing point on Santa Fe's Coleman Cutoff -- the Gulf-to-California short route -- as well as the end of this branch from Amarillo. headway_min and avg_speed_kmh are estimates, not read off a timetable.
sources: Segment-level: the June 5 1914 P&SF name change and lease of P&NT properties, and the 1911 and 1914 Coleman Cutoff line openings, are given in the TSHA entries for the P&SF and the P&NT; headway and speed are unsourced estimates.

segments.note: The P&NT was merged outright into the P&SF in 1948. By the early 1950s the Amarillo–Lubbock service was a single daily round trip worked by motor car -- trains 93 and 96, the westbound advertised as the West Texas Express and the eastbound as the Eastern Express, running as motor-trains with articulated motor car M-190. Stops: Canyon, Happy, Tulia, Kress, Plainview, Hale Center, Abernathy. headway_min and avg_speed_kmh are estimates, not read off a timetable.
sources: Segment-level: the 1948 P&NT merger is from the TSHA P&NT entry; the train numbers, the West Texas Express / Eastern Express names, the M-190 motor car and the station list are from the West Texas Express article. Headway is inferred from 'trains 93 and 96' being a single daily round trip, not read off a timetable; speed is an unsourced estimate.

segments.note: In 1955 train 96 was renumbered 94 and the pair went back to conventional locomotive haulage -- baggage car, lightweight coaches and sleepers, connecting at Amarillo with the San Francisco Chief. Trains 93-94 were discontinued June 19 1965, six weeks before the Panhandle and Santa Fe Railway itself was merged into the AT&SF on August 1 1965, so no era of this line was ever operated by the parent Santa Fe under its own name. Freight continues over the route today as BNSF's Plainview Subdivision -- context, not passenger service, and not drawn. headway_min and avg_speed_kmh are estimates, not read off a timetable.
sources: Segment-level: the 1955 renumbering, the change back to locomotive haulage, the San Francisco Chief connection at Amarillo and the June 19 1965 discontinuance are from the West Texas Express article; the August 1 1965 P&SF merger into the AT&SF is from the TSHA P&SF entry. Headway and speed are unsourced estimates.
